hero.title: A terminal that grew an IDE around your agents.
hero.lede: Run Claude Code, Codex, Pi or anything else in real terminals, on your machine or on any host over SSH, with the viewer, diagnostics, git, worktrees and databases they need to work.
hero.shotAlt: Remote Pi Cockpit as a multiplexed terminal: several real shells split across panes, with a workspace sidebar and file tree.

agents.title: Agents live in tabs.
agents.body: A tab is a real terminal, so you run the harness you already use: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Pi, OpenCode. Cockpit adds what a terminal never had. Each tab shows whether its agent is working, waiting on you or done, with a chime when the window is focused and a system notification when it is not, and Restart replaces the process in place, keeping the scrollback, the folder and the session it was running. Nothing to configure: a session started outside Cockpit simply reports nothing.
agents.shotAlt: An agent working in a Cockpit tab on a git worktree, with an inline green-and-red diff and new diagnostic issues reported.

remote.title: Your workspace, on any machine.
remote.p1: Open a folder on another computer and work in it exactly like a local one: the terminals, the file tree, the editor, source control and the databases all run on the host. A Raspberry Pi, an ARM VM, a beefy Linux box, a Mac or a Windows machine are all first-class hosts, from any client.
remote.p2: It is plain SSH, and SSH is the only door: Cockpit talks to a small cockpit-server on the host through a tunnel, with nothing exposed on the network. A new host shows you its fingerprint and asks; a host whose key changed is refused. A database password stays next to the database it opens, on the host, and never travels to your laptop.

sessions.title: Close the laptop. The agent keeps working.
sessions.body: Sessions belong to the host, not to the window you opened them from. Disconnect, walk away, come back from another machine, and the terminal picks up where it stopped. When the connection drops, a banner says so and Cockpit retries: the terminals freeze instead of dying.

vps.title: One curl turns a VPS into a host.
vps.body: No desktop, no sudo, idempotent, on Linux x86_64 and arm64. The flag --service registers a systemd --user unit so the host is ready right after a reboot; without it the client starts the server on demand over SSH.
vps.recipe: The whole recipe, including pinning a version and keeping the server in step with the app, is on the <download>download page</download> and in the <ref>remote hosts reference</ref>.

mobile.title: The same workspace, from a tablet.
mobile.p1: Cockpit on an iPad or an Android tablet is a pure remote client: it connects to a host and works there, so the agents run on a real machine while you drive them from the couch. Panels become drawers on a narrow screen, tabs scroll and reorder by touch, and a key bar gives you what a touch keyboard lacks: ESC, Tab, Ctrl+C, the arrows and F1 to F12, plus copy and paste.
mobile.p2: It ships as a direct Android APK, built and signed by the same release pipeline as the desktop builds. Grab it on the <download>download page</download>. Prepare the host first, from a desktop Cockpit or with the installer above.

documents.title: Your notes, requests and boards are tabs now.
documents.intro: Next to the terminal where your agent works, Cockpit opens the documents the work produces, and your agent writes to the same files:
documents.notebook: Notebook: a .notebook folder of plain markdown notes with tags, [[wiki links]], inline images and live formatting. Git, Obsidian and your agent see the same files, and cockpit note add lets the agent leave you one.
documents.http: HTTP requests: write one in the REST Client syntax in a .http file, press ⌘↵ and read the response as JSON, headers or raw text. cockpit http run fires the same request for the agent.
documents.kanban: Kanban boards with dependencies between cards, filters by title and label, drag and drop, and markdown in comments.
documents.mermaid: Mermaid diagrams rendered in the markdown preview, offline, in your theme.
documents.window: Document window: open any file in its own light window, from the app or straight from Finder, Explorer or your Linux file manager.
documents.gallery: Gallery: one click creates and opens any of them, on a local or a remote workspace.

secrets.title: Stop pasting tokens into your agent's prompt.
secrets.body: A .env.cockpit at the workspace root feeds every terminal Cockpit opens there, on local and remote workspaces alike. The values it injects are replaced by *** in the terminal, in the saved scrollback and in cockpit read-tab, so a secret does not reach the screen your agent is reading.
secrets.note: Keys that change who runs what are never injected (PATH, SHELL, HOME, LD_*, DYLD_* and friends), and when the file came with the repository, new terminals print a notice listing the key names it injected, never the values.

cli.title: The agent drives the cockpit.
cli.body: A built-in cockpit CLI, on the PATH of its terminals and nowhere else, lets an agent open tabs and splits, type into another tab, read what it printed, run your project's tasks, query your databases and write notes. Local or over SSH, always handled by the Cockpit that owns the tab. Database connections are read-only by default and can be hidden from the CLI entirely, so an agent queries what you allow.
cli.ref: Every command, flag, and id convention lives in the <ref>Cockpit reference</ref>.

ide.title: Viewer, diagnostics, git. When you need them.
ide.body: Syntax-highlighted code in ~190 languages, live diagnostics and formatting from any language server on your PATH (Dart, TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust and more), plus git status and one-click worktrees. The agent edits; you review.
ide.shotAlt: Cockpit's code viewer showing a Dart file with syntax highlighting, styled documentation comments, and a file path breadcrumb.

database.title: Databases as tabs.
database.body: SQLite, Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Redis and MongoDB: open them as tabs, query them, and let agents do the same through cockpit db.
database.shotAlt: Cockpit's Database panel listing Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Redis, MongoDB, and an auto-detected SQLite connection.

workspaces.title: Every context, one click away.
workspaces.body: Group projects into workspaces, workspaces into realms, and fork onto a fresh git worktree with your whole layout recreated. Point at a folder of repositories and you get a sectioned tree, an aggregate git badge and per-repo actions, locally and over SSH.

layouts.title: Your environment, in the repo.
layouts.body: A .ckp file describes the terminals a project opens (folders, splits, commands) and can apply itself to every new worktree. A .cockpit/tasks.json turns your dev servers into play and stop buttons with profiles and reload on save, on top of the tasks Cockpit already detects from package.json and pubspec.yaml.
layouts.tutorial: Build both from scratch in the <tutorial>layouts and tasks tutorial</tutorial>.

yours.title: Themes, sounds, your language.
yours.body: Nine built-in themes, or write your own: one JSON file paints the UI, the syntax highlighting and the terminal palette at once, inheriting everything you don't declare. Pick the terminal font family, bind a sound to each agent event (turn done, action needed, error), and read the whole interface in English, Portuguese or Spanish.

updates.title: Updates
updates.lede: How each platform gets the next version.
updates.p1: On macOS and Windows, Cockpit updates itself: it checks a signed appcast (Sparkle and WinSparkle), downloads the new build and restarts into it. You can keep the installer you downloaded once and never come back here.
updates.p2: On Linux there is no self-update. The app tells you when a release is out, and you install the new .deb or .rpm yourself, with Cockpit closed.
updates.foot: A remote host is separate: its cockpit-server has to run the same version as the app, so update it by re-running the installer. See the section below.

DownloadPage.foot: Cockpit is a terminal first: no account, no cloud, nothing else to install. Agents run as ordinary processes in its tabs, so you bring the harness you already use (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Pi, OpenCode). Every command and file format lives in the <docs>Cockpit reference</docs>.

vps.title: Put Cockpit on a machine with no desktop
vps.lede: One command turns a VPS, a build server or a Raspberry Pi into a host you can open as a remote workspace, and it is how the mobile client reaches a machine that no desktop has prepared before.
vps.installLede: Run this on the host, over SSH.
vps.installBody: The script detects the architecture, downloads the matching cockpit-server zip from the GitHub release, verifies its SHA-256 and installs into ~/.cockpit/server, linking the binary into ~/.local/bin. Nothing is exposed on the network: the app talks to it through an SSH tunnel.
vps.installFoot: Piping a script into bash deserves a look first: read the source of the installer (the short URL redirects to it), or download it, read it, and run it as a file.
vps.versionsBody: Client and server are released together, and the app refuses a host running a different version. Keep both on the same release, or pin the server with COCKPIT_VERSION={version}. A desktop client fixes a mismatch by itself over SSH; from the mobile client, re-run the installer on the host.
vps.foot: Start at boot needs linger on most distributions; the --service path tries to enable it and prints the one sudo line to run when it cannot. The full story, including how a desktop installs the server for you and what to do when a connection fails, is in the remote hosts reference.

WhyPage.title: Why Pi
WhyPage.metaDescription: Deciding how to run an always-on coding agent? remote-pi keeps Pi alive 24/7 and puts it in your pocket. Here's when that's the right shape — and when an all-in-one platform isn't.
WhyPage.h1: An always-on agent you assemble yourself.
WhyPage.lede: remote-pi turns Pi into a background agent that never logs off — and a phone in your pocket that drives it. This page is about that choice: keeping a coding agent alive 24/7, and whether building it up from something small is the shape you want.
WhyPage.gotTitle: Pi, kept alive and put in your pocket.
WhyPage.h1Desc: A per-machine supervisor (launchd on macOS, systemd on Linux) keeps every paired folder running as a background agent — survives logout, restarts on crash, answers at 3am.
WhyPage.h2Desc: Pi is a small coding agent, not a platform. It boots fast and runs only what you add to it — nothing you didn't ask for.
WhyPage.h3Desc: Extend Pi with the skills, plugins, and per-folder agents you actually need. The agent is yours to shape until it fits your work exactly.
WhyPage.h4Desc: Pair once with a QR. Send prompts, switch models, start a fresh session, or compact context from iOS or Android — wherever you are.
WhyPage.h5Title: A mesh when you need it
WhyPage.h5Desc: Agents reach each other on one machine over a local socket, or across PCs through the relay. One Owner key, one mesh, no central server.
WhyPage.h6Desc: MIT licensed. Run the community relay or host your own; traffic is encrypted in transit, and self-hosting keeps it on infrastructure you control.
WhyPage.honestTitle: What about OpenClaw and Hermes Agent?
WhyPage.honestP1: They're excellent. OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are first-class always-on, open-source agents. If you want a batteries-included platform that ships ready to run, you should look hard at them — this page won't pretend otherwise.
WhyPage.honestP2: remote-pi makes a different bet. It starts from Pi — a lightweight coding agent — and adds just the always-on layer: a supervisor that keeps it running and a phone that drives it. Everything else, you assemble. The trade is real: less out of the box, more that's exactly yours.
WhyPage.choiceBody: Want a complete, all-in-one platform, ready out of the box? OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are great places to start. Want a lightweight coding agent you assemble, keep alive 24/7, and control from your phone? That's Pi with remote-pi.
WhyPage.scopeNote: One note on scope: this comparison is about the always-on layer — remote-pi's daemon mode — not coding agents in general. It's the part where keeping an agent alive and reachable is the whole job, and where OpenClaw and Hermes Agent shine too.
WhyPage.getStartedTitle: Build yours and leave it running.
WhyPage.getStartedSub: Add the plugin to Pi, pair your phone, and promote a folder to a 24/7 daemon. The how-to walks every step.

PrivacyPage.s2P1: Remote Pi is designed so that you provide essentially nothing to us on the relay path. There is no account, no email registration, no profile, and no payment information. The pairing flow generates cryptographic keys locally on your devices.
PrivacyPage.s2P2: On the device itself, the mobile app stores a list of paired peers (their public keys, a friendly name you choose, and the relay URL) in the platform's secure storage (iOS Keychain / Android Keystore). This information never leaves your device unless you explicitly send it.
PrivacyPage.s2h2: 2.2 Data processed automatically by the public relay
PrivacyPage.s2P3: When you connect to the public relay operated by Flutterando, the relay processes three categories of data:
PrivacyPage.s2Li1: Connection metadata — source IP address, connection timestamps, public-key identifier of the connecting peer, room identifiers, and basic transport statistics (bytes in/out, message timing and sizes). This is logged for at most 30 days and used for abuse mitigation and reliable operation of the relay.
PrivacyPage.s2Li2: Message payloads forwarded between paired peers. In the current MVP, payloads travel base64-encoded over TLS and are not end-to-end encrypted at the application layer. The relay operator could in principle access plaintext message contents in memory while forwarding. We do not log, persist, or inspect those payloads — we forward them and discard them. See §9 for the full trust model.
PrivacyPage.s2Li3: Signed mesh-membership blobs. When you pair a new machine, your Owner key signs a small JSON blob listing which Pi devices belong to that Owner's mesh, and your app uploads it to the relay via POST /mesh/<owner_pk_hash>. The relay verifies the Ed25519 signature and persists the blob (a few KB per Owner) so that new devices restoring the same Owner key can recover their peer list. The blob contains: Owner public key, a version number, the list of Pi public keys you have paired, and a timestamp. It is not encrypted — anyone with access to the relay database can read it. Pairing on your own self-hosted relay keeps this data on your infrastructure.
PrivacyPage.s2P4: If you require cryptographic confidentiality from the relay operator, self-host the relay (the code is open source and documented). When you self-host, the data described in §2.2 is processed by your own infrastructure, not by Flutterando.
PrivacyPage.s2Li5: Contacts, photos, microphone, or camera content.
PrivacyPage.s2Li6: The text of your prompts or the responses produced by your Pi-side agent.
PrivacyPage.s3P1: The limited connection metadata described in §2.2 is used to:
PrivacyPage.s3Li1: Operate, maintain, and route traffic on the relay service.
PrivacyPage.s3Li2: Detect and mitigate abuse, such as denial-of-service attacks or patterns of unauthorized access attempts.
PrivacyPage.s3Li3: Investigate incidents and protect the security of the Service and its users.
PrivacyPage.s3P2: We do not use any data for advertising, profiling, or behavioral analytics.
PrivacyPage.s4P1: Under the Brazilian General Data Protection Law (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados, Law 13.709/2018, "LGPD"), we process the limited data described above on the following legal bases:
PrivacyPage.s4Li1: Performance of a contract (Article 7, V) — to provide the relay service you connect to.
PrivacyPage.s4Li2: Legitimate interest (Article 7, IX) — to ensure the security and integrity of the relay infrastructure.
PrivacyPage.s5P1: We do not sell or rent your data. We do not share connection metadata with third parties for advertising or analytics purposes. We may disclose data only when required to do so by a valid legal order under Brazilian law, and only to the extent strictly necessary to comply with that order.
PrivacyPage.s5P2: If you choose to self-host your own relay or connect to a relay operated by a third party, that operator becomes the data controller for the connection metadata they process. This Policy does not cover third-party relays.
PrivacyPage.s6P1: The public relay operated by Flutterando may be hosted in data centers located outside Brazil. Where this is the case, transfers occur under conditions equivalent to those required by Article 33 of the LGPD, including contractual safeguards with infrastructure providers. You can avoid international transfer entirely by running your own relay on infrastructure under your control.
PrivacyPage.s7P1: Relay connection logs are retained for a maximum of 30 days, after which they are deleted or anonymized. Aggregated, non-identifying statistics (e.g. daily active connection counts) may be retained longer for capacity planning.
PrivacyPage.s7P2: Paired peers stored on your device persist until you revoke the pairing or uninstall the app. We do not have access to that storage.
PrivacyPage.s8P1: Subject to the LGPD, you have the right to request, with respect to personal data we hold about you:
PrivacyPage.s8Li1: Confirmation that we process your data.
PrivacyPage.s8Li3: Correction of incomplete, inaccurate, or outdated data.
PrivacyPage.s8Li4: Anonymization, blocking, or deletion of unnecessary or excessive data, or data processed in non-compliance with the LGPD.
PrivacyPage.s8Li5: Information about public and private entities with which we have shared your data.
PrivacyPage.s8Li6: Information about the possibility of not providing consent, and the consequences of refusal.
PrivacyPage.s8Li7: Revocation of consent, where consent was the legal basis.
PrivacyPage.s8P2: To exercise any of these rights, contact our DPO at <link>{email}</link>. We may need to verify your identity (for example, by asking you to prove control of a paired device's public key) before fulfilling the request.
PrivacyPage.s9Li1: TLS 1.3 on every connection between clients and the relay.
PrivacyPage.s9Li2: Ed25519 challenge-response at pairing time, so paired devices verify each other's identity cryptographically and identity squatting is prevented.
PrivacyPage.s9Li3: Private keys generated on-device and stored in the platform secure storage (iOS Keychain / Android Keystore). Private keys never leave your devices.
PrivacyPage.s9Li4: Operational separation between transport metadata and any other system, with strict access controls on relay logs.
PrivacyPage.s9P2: Important — read this if confidentiality matters to you. Application-layer end-to-end encryption of message payloads is not active in the current MVP. Payloads travel base64-encoded over TLS to the relay and from the relay to the paired device. The public relay operator (Flutterando) could in principle access plaintext message contents in memory while forwarding, but we do not log, persist, or inspect payloads. Per-message end-to-end encryption was removed for MVP stability and is on the roadmap for a future release.
PrivacyPage.s9P3: If you require cryptographic confidentiality from the relay operator, run your own relay. The relay is open source and the documentation covers Docker deployment and VPN gating (Tailscale, WireGuard) so that only your devices can reach the relay's WebSocket port at all.
PrivacyPage.s9P4: No system is perfectly secure. If you believe your account or device has been compromised, revoke the affected pairing immediately and report the incident to <link>{email}</link>.

intro.p1: This is the <strong1>reference</strong1>. Remote Pi is a mesh for coding agents: agents on the same machine talk through a local UDS broker, agents on different machines reach each other through an open-source relay, and your phone authenticates new peers and drives sessions. The first supported harness is the <a1>Pi coding agent</a1>; <code1>/remote-pi</code1> wires everything up. To <strong1>learn by doing</strong1>, start with the <link1>tutorials</link1>; for <strong1>why</strong1> it works this way, see <link2>Why Pi</link2>. The pages below are for looking things up.

quickStart.title: Quick start
quickStart.p1: Install the plugin, run the setup wizard, and pair your phone in a few commands — then send your first prompt from the app. The full walkthrough, including the mobile side, is a tutorial.

whatItDoes.title: What it does
whatItDoes.p1: Remote Pi adds two independent layers on top of Pi. The <strong1>agent network</strong1> lets agents discover and message each other — over a local socket on one machine, or through the relay across PCs. The <strong1>mobile control plane</strong1> is your phone: it authenticates new peers into the mesh and drives sessions. Each is covered hands-on:
whatItDoes.li1: <link3>Local mesh</link3> — agents discovering and messaging on the same machine.
whatItDoes.li2: <link4>Remote mesh</link4> — routing between agents on different PCs.
whatItDoes.li3: <link5>Getting started</link5> — pairing your phone and driving an agent from it.

install.title: Install
install.p1: Requirements: Node 20+ and Pi (the host coding agent). Remote Pi installs as a Pi plugin with <code1>pi install npm:remote-pi</code1>, which self-registers the <code1>/remote-pi</code1> slash command and deploys the agent-network skill. The complete setup — wizard, pairing, first command — is in the tutorial.
install.p2: → <link5>See the Getting started tutorial</link5>. Daemon mode has its own one-time install — see <a2>Daemon mode</a2> below.

usingRemotePi.title: Using /remote-pi
usingRemotePi.p1: <code1>/remote-pi</code1> is the everyday entry point. The first run opens a short wizard (agent name, whether to use the relay) that creates the per-folder config; later runs join the local mesh and start the relay automatically. Re-run the wizard with <code1>/remote-pi setup</code1>. Every subcommand is in the <a3>command reference</a3>.
usingRemotePi.p2: → <link5>See the Getting started tutorial</link5> for the guided flow.

pairing.title: Pairing a mobile device
pairing.p1: <code1>/remote-pi pair</code1> prints a QR (and a copy-paste URI); scan it with the Remote Pi app. Pairing is <strong1>per machine</strong1> — once a device is paired, every Pi process on that machine accepts it. Manage devices with <code1>/remote-pi devices</code1> and <code1>/remote-pi revoke '<'shortid'>'</code1> (see the <a3>command reference</a3>).

quickActions.title: Quick actions from the phone
quickActions.p1: Beyond chatting, the app drives a session with a small set of typed actions — <strong1>compact context</strong1>, <strong1>new session</strong1>, <strong1>set model</strong1>, and <strong1>set thinking</strong1> level. The model picker reads live from the host, so it always reflects what that machine can run. The full vocabulary, wire format, and fallback semantics live in <a4>PROTOCOL.md</a4> (the <em1>App actions</em1> section).

agentNetwork.title: Agent network
agentNetwork.p1: Each agent is a peer in a mesh. The LLM gets three tools — <code1>list_peers</code1> (who is online), <code1>agent_send</code1> (send with an ACK), and <code1>get_messages</code1> (drain the inbox). On one machine, peers talk over a Unix-domain-socket broker; across machines, the same <code1>agent_send</code1> routes through the relay, addressing remote peers as <code1>pc_label:peer</code1>. Both paths are covered hands-on:
agentNetwork.li1: <link3>Local mesh</link3> — the broker, the three tools, a concrete exchange.
agentNetwork.li2: <link4>Remote mesh</link4> — cross-PC addressing and what an ACK does (and doesn't) guarantee.

daemonMode.title: Daemon mode
daemonMode.p1: Promote a folder to a 24/7 background agent: run <code1>/remote-pi install</code1> once per machine to install the supervisor (launchd on macOS, <code1>systemd --user</code1> on Linux) and link the CLI, then <code1>remote-pi create '<'folder'>' --name "…"</code1> to register and start a daemon. One supervisor per machine, N daemons under it. Every command is in the <a3>command reference</a3> below.
daemonMode.p2: → <link6>See the Daemon mode tutorial</link6> for the full how-to; the <em1>why</em1> (and how it compares to all-in-one platforms) is <link2>Why Pi</link2>.

relay.title: The relay
relay.p1: The relay is the only network-touching piece of Remote Pi. In the current MVP it sees both message payloads (forwarded but never logged or inspected by the community operator) and connection metadata: which keypair is online, which room/cwd identifiers exist, message timing, sizes. Traffic is encrypted in transit (TLS) and peers authenticate with Ed25519 pairing, but payloads are not encrypted at the application layer — see <a5>Protocol & Security</a5> and the Privacy Policy, section 9, for the full picture.
relay.p2: The relay also <strong1>persists a small SQLite table</strong1> called <code1>mesh_versions</code1> — blobs signed by your Owner key listing the Pi devices that belong to your mesh (a few KB per Owner). The relay verifies the Ed25519 signature on every <code1>POST /mesh/'<'owner_pk_hash'>'</code1> and stores what you signed; it never decides membership itself. New devices restoring your Owner key recover their peer list from this blob. A relay compromise means DoS, not impersonation. See the <a4>PROTOCOL.md</a4> mesh-membership section for the wire format.

relay_communityRelay.title: Option A — Use the community relay
relay_communityRelay.p1: <code1>https://relay-rp1.jacobmoura.work</code1> (default). Zero setup. Good for trying things out or for casual use. (Internally the extension uses the WebSocket form <code1>wss://…</code1> — both schemes point at the same endpoint.)
relay_communityRelay.li2: <strong1>TLS in transit is the only network protection</strong1> — the relay operator sees plaintext envelopes (payloads, routing metadata, peer pubkeys, timing). Self-host for confidentiality from the operator.
relay_communityRelay.li3: <strong1>No IP allow-listing or VPN gating</strong1> built in. Anyone with a paired keypair can connect; layer a VPN on top via Option B if you want network-level isolation.

relay_selfHost.title: Option B — Self-host (recommended for privacy)
relay_selfHost.p1: Run the relay yourself in Docker and put it behind a VPN like <a6>Tailscale</a6>, <a7>WireGuard</a7>, or your own VPC. Because the relay's network-level protection is just TLS + keypair authentication, layering a VPN on top means <strong1>only your devices</strong1> can even reach the WebSocket port — defense in depth.
relay_selfHost.p2: Quick Docker outline (see the <a8>relay README</a8> for the full setup, environment variables, and reverse-proxy guidance):
relay_selfHost.p3: The <code1>-v remote-pi-data:/data</code1> mount is required — that's where the relay keeps <code1>mesh.db</code1> (the Owner-signed mesh blobs). Skip the volume and the table is wiped on every container restart, forcing every client to re-publish.
relay_selfHost.p4: The relay serves the WebSocket upgrade, <code1>/health</code1>, and <code1>/mesh/'<'owner_pk_hash'>'</code1> on the same port (default 3000) — point your reverse proxy at one upstream and you're done. Use <code1>/health</code1> for liveness probes (Coolify, Kubernetes, Fly health checks).
relay_selfHost.p5: Bind the container to your VPN interface, terminate TLS in a reverse proxy, and point both your Pi and your phone at the resulting <code1>https://…</code1> URL.

relay_pointPi.p1: Once your relay is reachable, tell the extension:
relay_pointPi.p2: The URL must be <code1>http://</code1> or <code1>https://</code1> — <code1>wss://</code1> / <code1>ws://</code1> are rejected at validation. The extension converts to the WebSocket form internally when it opens the connection, so you can paste whatever URL your reverse proxy or PaaS dashboard exposes.
relay_pointPi.p3: This writes <code1>~/.pi/remote/config.json</code1> with <code1>'{' "relay": "..." '}'</code1>. Resolution order (highest precedence first):
relay_pointPi.p4: Verify the active URL and its source with:
relay_pointPi.p5: To switch URLs while connected: <code1>/remote-pi stop</code1> then <code1>/remote-pi</code1> again. The mobile app has its own relay-URL setting in its preferences pane — keep both pointing at the same relay.

protocol.title: Protocol & Security
protocol.p1: The canonical spec for everything wire-level — envelope format, identity model (Owner key + per-device subkeys), ACK protocol, cross-PC routing, mesh membership, trust model, and failure modes — lives in <a4>PROTOCOL.md</a4> on GitHub. It is the source of truth that the Pi extension, the mobile apps, and the relay all implement against. Read it when you need exact behavior or when writing a new harness adapter.
protocol.p2: <strong1>Security posture, in short.</strong1> Connections to the relay are <strong1>encrypted in transit (TLS)</strong1>, and devices authenticate each other with <strong1>Ed25519 pairing</strong1>, so paired peers verify identity cryptographically. Message payloads are <strong1>not</strong1> encrypted at the application layer — the relay operator could in principle read plaintext in memory while forwarding. If you need confidentiality from the relay operator, <a9>self-host the relay</a9> behind a VPN. The Privacy Policy, section 9, restates this in plain language, and PROTOCOL.md is the deep dive that matches the code.

commands.title: Command reference
commands.p1: Every command works as a Pi slash command (interactive) and as a shell-level <code1>remote-pi '<'subcommand'>'</code1> when the package is installed globally (<code1>npm install -g remote-pi</code1>).
commands.p2: The footer in the Pi TUI reflects state live:
commands.li1: <code1>📡 local (N)</code1> — local mesh session and peer count
commands.li2: <code1>🟢 relay</code1> — relay connected, at least one device paired on this machine
commands.li3: <code1>🟡 relay waiting for pairing</code1> — relay connected, no device paired yet
commands.li4: <code1>📱 '<'shortid'>'</code1> — a mobile device is actively connected right now
commands.p3: The window title is two parts — <code1>'<'agent-name'>' · On</code1> when the relay is up or <code1>'<'agent-name'>' · Off</code1> otherwise — so you can tell your terminal tabs apart at a glance.

commands_commandsLocal.td1: Connect (join local mesh + start relay), or run setup on first use
commands_commandsLocal.td2: Run the setup wizard and update local config
commands_commandsLocal.td4: List local and cross-PC mesh peers, grouped by PC label

commands_commandsLocal.td7: Revoke a paired device by its shortid (brings the relay up first, like pair, to notify the device)
commands_commandsLocal.td8: Persist a new relay URL (http:// or https://)

commands_commandsDaemon.title: Daemon fleet — one supervisor, N background Pis
commands_commandsDaemon.p1: See <a2>Daemon mode</a2> for the overview and the <link6>Daemon mode tutorial</link6> for the full how-to.
commands_commandsDaemon.td1: Register a folder as a daemon (starts it when the supervisor is running)
commands_commandsDaemon.td4: Start one daemon by id, or every registered daemon with no id
commands_commandsDaemon.cell1: Stop one daemon by id, or every running daemon with no id (<code1>/remote-pi stop</code1> stops only the local terminal)
commands_commandsDaemon.td5: Restart one daemon by id, or every daemon with no id
commands_commandsDaemon.td6: Detailed runtime status (pid, uptime, restart count)
commands_commandsDaemon.td7: Send a prompt to a specific daemon
commands_commandsDaemon.cell2: Install <code1>pi-supervisord</code1> as a system service <strong1>and</strong1> symlink the <code1>remote-pi</code1> CLI into <code1>~/.local/bin/</code1>
commands_commandsDaemon.cell3: Remove the system service <strong1>and</strong1> the <code1>~/.local/bin</code1> symlinks (daemon registry preserved)

commands_commandsCron.title: Daemon cron — scheduled prompts
commands_commandsCron.p1: Schedule recurring prompts to a daemon. The scheduler runs <strong1>inside the supervisor</strong1>, so it only fires when the supervisor is installed as a service (<a2>Daemon mode</a2> / <code1>/remote-pi install</code1>) — otherwise <code1>cron add</code1> warns instead of scheduling. See the <link7>Daemon mode tutorial</link7> for the walkthrough.
commands_commandsCron.td1: Schedule a recurring prompt to a daemon (5-field cron expression; runs must be ≥60s apart)
commands_commandsCron.td2: List jobs: schedule, enabled, last run / status, next run
commands_commandsCron.td3: Fire a job now, ignoring its schedule
commands_commandsCron.td5: Pause a job without deleting it
commands_commandsCron.cell1: Tail the fire / skip audit log (default N = 20), optionally for one job
commands_commandsCron.li1: <strong1>Minimum interval 60s.</strong1> A more frequent expression is rejected (each fire spends tokens). Croner syntax — five fields (<code1>min hour day-of-month month day-of-week</code1>), plus an optional seconds field, still bounded by the 60s floor.
commands_commandsCron.li2: <strong1>Timezone per job.</strong1> <code1>--tz Area/City</code1> resolves DST; without it a job runs in the machine's local time.
commands_commandsCron.li3: <strong1>Overlap & downtime.</strong1> A fire is skipped while the daemon is mid-turn (<code1>--no-skip-busy</code1> overrides), skipped if the daemon is down (<code1>--wake</code1> starts it first), and at most one missed run is replayed on startup (<code1>--catchup</code1>, off by default).
commands_commandsCron.li4: <strong1>Audit.</strong1> Every fire <em1>and</em1> every skip appends one line to <code1>~/.pi/remote/cron.jsonl</code1> with a <code1>result</code1> of <code1>delivered</code1>, <code1>deliver_failed</code1>, <code1>woke_and_delivered</code1>, <code1>skipped_busy</code1>, <code1>skipped_down</code1>, or <code1>skipped_disabled</code1>. The agent's reply itself is fire-and-forget into the mesh — cron records the trigger, not the response.

config.title: Configuration files
config.cell2: Daemon registry (list of <code1>'{' cwd, name '}'</code1> entries)
config.cell3: Pi-secret fallback when the OS keyring is unavailable (headless Linux). Stored with <code1>chmod 0600</code1>. See <a4>PROTOCOL.md</a4> for the keyring details.
config.p1: Override the relay for a single run without persisting:
config.p2: Only <code1>http://</code1> / <code1>https://</code1> are accepted — <code1>wss://</code1> / <code1>ws://</code1> are rejected at validation, the extension converts to the WebSocket form internally when it opens the connection.
config.p3: Daemons don't read the per-directory file at all — the supervisor injects their whole config inline via the <code1>REMOTE_PI_DIRECT_CONFIG</code1> environment variable at spawn (a fixed <code1>assistent</code1> workspace with the relay on), so a daemon folder needs no <code1>.pi/remote-pi/</code1> of its own. You can set the same variable yourself to override <code1>'<'cwd'>'/.pi/remote-pi/config.json</code1> for a single run — an escape hatch for CI, ops, and the Cockpit desktop client:

troubleshooting_footerStuck.title: Footer says 🟡 relay waiting for pairing even though I paired a device
troubleshooting_footerStuck.p1: The icon reflects whether <em1>any</em1> device has been paired on this machine, not whether one is connected right now. If you really have a paired device in <code1>/remote-pi devices</code1>, restart Pi — the cache may be stale (fixed in current release; report a bug if it recurs).

troubleshooting_timeoutMobile.title: Mobile app times out connecting
troubleshooting_timeoutMobile.p1: Verify the same relay URL is configured on both sides. If you self-host behind a VPN, your phone must also be on the VPN (Tailscale on iOS/Android works fine).

troubleshooting_timeoutRequest.title: Reply never arrives
troubleshooting_timeoutRequest.p1: <code1>agent_send</code1> returned <code1>'{' status: "received" '}'</code1> but no reply ever lands in your inbox. Possible causes:
troubleshooting_timeoutRequest.li1: <strong1>Receiver crashed or never processed.</strong1> Run <code1>/remote-pi peers</code1> to see whether the peer is still online.
troubleshooting_timeoutRequest.li2: <strong1>The receiver chose not to reply.</strong1> <code1>agent_send</code1> is not RPC — there's no obligation to respond. If the conversation needs a reply, the prompt to the receiver must say so explicitly.
troubleshooting_timeoutRequest.li3: <strong1>Cross-PC: peer went offline.</strong1> Look in your inbox for a <code1>transport_error</code1> envelope with <code1>re='<'your-send-id'>'</code1> — the relay returns one when a forwarded message can't be delivered. A <code1>Delivered</code1> ACK only means the remote broker accepted the envelope, not that the peer is alive — validate by roundtrip.
troubleshooting_timeoutRequest.p2: <strong1>Note:</strong1> <code1>agent_request</code1> is deprecated (still available as a wrapper for backward compat, emits a warning). New agents call <code1>agent_send</code1> and observe the inbox in a future turn.

troubleshooting_onePiPerCwd.title: Two Pi processes can't share a directory
troubleshooting_onePiPerCwd.p1: A cwd lock allows <strong1>one Pi process per directory</strong1>. If you try to run <code1>/remote-pi</code1> in a second terminal that's already in the same folder, the second start is rejected (and the relay, separately, refuses a duplicate room with <code1>RoomAlreadyOpenError</code1>).
troubleshooting_onePiPerCwd.p2: <strong1>To run two agents side by side:</strong1> put them in two different directories — each gets its own workspace and both meet in the same <code1>local</code1> session. See the <link3>Local mesh tutorial</link3>.
troubleshooting_onePiPerCwd.p3: If you actually wanted a second terminal at the same workspace (e.g. just to read state), stop the running Pi first or open a shell that does <em1>not</em1> launch Pi.

intro.p1: Everything the desktop app reads from your repository or writes to your machine: the internal <code1>cockpit</code1> CLI that agents use to drive tabs, the <code1>.ckp</code1> pane layouts, the <code1>.cockpit/tasks.json</code1> Task Run file, the theme format, the documents that open as tabs, the <code1>.env.cockpit</code1> that feeds your terminals, and the harness hooks behind the turn status. For the product tour, see the <link1>Cockpit page</link1>; for the mesh, daemons, and the relay, see the <link2>Remote Pi docs</link2>.

install.title: Install
install.p1: Cockpit ships for macOS, Windows, and Linux. macOS builds are signed and notarized, and every platform that supports it gets in-app updates. Grab a build from the <link3>download page</link3> — <code1>.dmg</code1>, <code1>.exe</code1>, <code1>.deb</code1> and <code1>.rpm</code1> (x64 and arm64), each with a published SHA-256.
install.p2: Cockpit is a terminal first: it needs no account, no cloud and nothing else installed to be useful. Agents run as ordinary processes in its tabs, so the harness you already use (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Pi, OpenCode) is the one that runs here.
install.p3: Working on another machine is SSH plus <code1>cockpit-server</code1>, described in <a1>Remote hosts & VPS</a1>. That is unrelated to the Remote Pi relay: the mesh, the phone app and the 24/7 daemons belong to the <link4>Remote Pi project</link4> and are not part of Cockpit.

cli.title: The cockpit CLI
cli.p1: Cockpit materializes a small binary at <code1>~/.cockpit/bin/cockpit</code1> and puts that folder on the <code1>PATH</code1> of the terminals it spawns — and only those. So the CLI exists for anything running inside Cockpit (you, a script, an agent) and does not leak into the rest of your shell environment. It talks to the app over a local socket: a Unix socket on macOS and Linux, a loopback TCP port plus a token on Windows.
cli.p2: This is what makes Cockpit an <em1>agentic</em1> multiplexer: an agent in one tab can open another tab, type into it, read what it printed, run a project task, or query a database — the same verbs a human uses, with no screen scraping.

cli_cliTargets.title: Targets & ids
cli_cliTargets.p1: The unit the CLI addresses is a <strong1>tab</strong1> (one terminal or agent session). A <strong1>pane</strong1> is the split leaf that groups tabs and is not addressable — <code1>list-panes</code1> and <code1>read-pane</code1> survive as legacy aliases.
cli_cliTargets.cell1: Target another tab. Defaults to <code1>$COCKPIT_TAB_ID</code1> (the current tab; legacy fallback <code1>$COCKPIT_PANE_ID</code1>).
cli_cliTargets.cell2: Target whatever tab you are looking at, resolved by the app. Works from outside a Cockpit terminal too (dictation tools, scripts): with no env inherited the CLI finds the app through <code1>~/.cockpit/status.sock</code1>. Wins over <code1>--tab-id</code1>.
cli_cliTargets.cell3: (<code1>send</code1> only) press Enter right after the text, as a separate keystroke — a <code1>send</code1> plus a <code1>send-key Enter</code1> in one call.
cli_cliTargets.p2: Ids (<code1>t0</code1>, <code1>t1</code1>…) are assigned per app boot, so never hardcode one. Discover them with <code1>cockpit list-tabs</code1>, or give a tab a <strong1>stable label</strong1> (double-click the tab, or <code1>new-tab --title</code1>) and address it by name. Labels persist across boots; workspace ids are opaque UUIDs, so use <code1>workspacePath</code1> / <code1>path</code1> when you need the folder on disk.

cli_cliCommands.title: Command reference
cli_cliCommands.cell1: Press named keys: <code1>Enter Tab Escape Space BSpace Up Down Left Right Home End PageUp PageDown Delete</code1> and <code1>C-'<'letter'>'</code1> (e.g. <code1>C-c</code1>).
cli_cliCommands.cell2: Open a file in the app's viewer. Bare <code1>cockpit '<'file'>'</code1> is a shortcut for it, relative to the tab's cwd.
cli_cliCommands.cell3: Open a terminal tab and print its id. <code1>h</code1>/<code1>right</code1> splits side by side, <code1>v</code1>/<code1>down</code1> stacks; omit to open as a tab in the same pane. Anchored at the emitting tab's pane.
cli_cliCommands.cell4: Read a tab's rendered output. No target = the current tab. Alias: <code1>read-pane</code1>.
cli_cliCommands.td2: Read a task's output, even with no tab open for it.
cli_cliCommands.cell5: List active tabs (alias: <code1>list-panes</code1>). The JSON carries <code1>label</code1>, <code1>workspacePath</code1>, <code1>working</code1> and, for task output tabs, <code1>taskId</code1>.
cli_cliCommands.cell6: List this workspace's tasks. <code1>[output]</code1> marks tasks whose output <code1>read-task</code1> can read (ran this boot); ● marks tasks running right now.
cli_cliCommands.cell7: SQL databases registered in the workspace — see <a2>Databases</a2>.
cli_cliCommands.td4: Run a Redis command, or open the key table for a human.
cli_cliCommands.td5: Run a MongoDB command, or open the collection browser.
cli_cliCommands.cell8: Apply a pane layout — see <a3><code1>.ckp</code1> layouts</a3>.
cli_cliCommands.td6: Install the Claude Code skill that teaches this CLI.

cli_cliRead.title: Reading output
cli_cliRead.p1: <code1>read-tab</code1> and <code1>read-task</code1> share a windowing model. Output is always chronological (top to bottom); the flags only pick which window you get.
cli_cliRead.td1: How many lines to return (server cap: 2000).
cli_cliRead.td2: Skip N lines from the anchor — this is your pagination.
cli_cliRead.td4: Anchor at the start of the buffer instead of the tail.
cli_cliRead.p2: Task ids are stable per workspace: <code1>npm:'<'script'>'</code1> from <code1>package.json</code1>, <code1>flutter:run</code1> / <code1>flutter:test</code1>, and <code1>json:'<'label'>'</code1> from <code1>.cockpit/tasks.json</code1>.

layouts.title: .ckp pane layouts
layouts.p1: A <code1>.ckp</code1> file is a versionable YAML that describes the terminals to open in a workspace — the equivalent of a tmuxinator layout. One file is one layout, and the file name is the layout name (<code1>dev.ckp</code1> → layout “dev”). Commit it, and a teammate gets your working geometry on clone.
layouts.p2: There are three ways to apply one:
layouts.li1: <strong1>GUI</strong1> — right-click the <code1>.ckp</code1> file in the tree → <strong1>Open layout</strong1>.
layouts.li2: <strong1>CLI</strong1> — <code1>cockpit orchestrate dev.ckp</code1> from inside a tab.
layouts.li3: <strong1>Worktree autorun</strong1> — <code1>autorun: worktree</code1> in the file: the layout is applied by itself whenever you create a worktree of the workspace. The worktree is born empty, so the geometry comes out exact.

layouts_layoutsFields.title: Fields
layouts_layoutsFields.p1: <strong1>Root:</strong1> <code1>panes</code1> (required) is the list of panes in creation order. <code1>autorun</code1> (optional) accepts only <code1>worktree</code1>; with two or more autorun files at the root, none of them runs — ambiguity is never guessed.
layouts_layoutsFields.td2: Unique (case-insensitive). Becomes the tab's manual label and the merge key.
layouts_layoutsFields.cell1: Relative to the file's folder, forward slashes only. Absolute paths and <code1>\</code1> are rejected for portability.
layouts_layoutsFields.cell2: Where it is born, relative to the <em1>previously created</em1> pane: <code1>tab</code1>, <code1>right</code1>, <code1>down</code1>.
layouts_layoutsFields.td6: Typed into the terminal and run by the tab's shell (resolved through the machine's PATH).
layouts_layoutsFields.cell3: <code1>macos</code1> / <code1>windows</code1> / <code1>linux</code1>, string or list — same semantics as in <code1>tasks.json</code1>.

layouts_layoutsMerge.title: Replace semantics
layouts_layoutsMerge.li1: Opening a layout means <strong1>become this layout</strong1>: the file is validated first, then every tab of the workspace is closed (pinned ones included), then the panes are built with exact geometry. If any tab has work running (an agent mid-turn, a process in a terminal, a live task) the GUI asks before closing; idle tabs close silently.
layouts_layoutsMerge.li2: <code1>cockpit orchestrate dev.ckp</code1> replaces without asking and keeps only the tab that ran the command. Pass <code1>--append</code1> to keep the old additive behavior: panes whose <code1>name</code1> already exists are skipped and nothing is closed. The worktree autorun always appends (the worktree is born empty, so it makes no difference).
layouts_layoutsMerge.li3: A missing <code1>cwd</code1> or invalid YAML gives a readable error (dialog in the GUI, stderr in the CLI); nothing is applied halfway from the failing pane on.
layouts_layoutsMerge.li4: <code1>command</code1> is typed ~700 ms after the tab opens, so the shell has time to finish booting, with Enter at the end.
layouts_layoutsMerge.p1: Cockpit treats <code1>.ckp</code1> as YAML for highlighting and shows the Cockpit logo as the file icon in the tree.

tasks.title: Task Run
tasks.p1: Task Run executes your project's build and dev commands (<code1>npm run dev</code1>, <code1>flutter run</code1>, <code1>go run</code1>, <code1>make</code1>…) with streamed output, a visual lifecycle (play / stop / restart), interactive keys, and reload-on-save. Two sources coexist:
tasks.li1: <strong1>Auto-detected</strong1> — on opening a project, Cockpit reads the manifests (<code1>package.json</code1> scripts, <code1>pubspec.yaml</code1>) and shows tasks with no config at all.
tasks.li2: <strong1>Declared</strong1> — <code1>.cockpit/tasks.json</code1>, for customizing, adding tasks, or describing a monorepo. JSON tasks take precedence over a detected task with the same id.
tasks.p2: It knows only <code1>command</code1>, <code1>args</code1>, and <code1>env</code1>. There are no stack-specific keys (flavor, dart-define, <code1>NODE_ENV</code1>) — all of that is expressed as <code1>args</code1> and <code1>env</code1>.

tasks_tasksFile.title: Where the file lives
tasks_tasksFile.p1: At the <strong1>root of the workspace you open</strong1>. Discovery is literal — Cockpit does not walk up the tree. For a single package, open the package folder. For a <strong1>monorepo</strong1>, open the root and let one <code1>.cockpit/tasks.json</code1> drive the subpackages through a per-task <code1>cwd</code1>.
tasks_tasksFile.p2: The file is <strong1>JSONC</strong1>: comments (<code1>//</code1> and <code1>/* */</code1>) and trailing commas are allowed, just like VSCode's <code1>tasks.json</code1>. Point <code1>$schema</code1> at <a4><code1>docs/tasks.schema.json</code1></a4> for editor autocomplete; Cockpit ignores the field when running.

tasks_tasksFields.title: Fields
tasks_tasksFields.p1: Root: <code1>tasks</code1> (required) and <code1>cwd</code1> (optional) — a default <code1>cwd</code1> for every task, which each task may override.
tasks_tasksFields.cell1: Short display name. The task id is derived from it: <code1>json:'<'label'>'</code1>.
tasks_tasksFields.td5: Base args, placed before the profile's args.
tasks_tasksFields.cell2: Run folder, relative to the <code1>tasks.json</code1> folder (absolute also accepted). Falls back to the top-level <code1>cwd</code1>, then the root.
tasks_tasksFields.cell3: OSes where the task is visible: <code1>macos</code1>, <code1>windows</code1>, <code1>linux</code1>.
tasks_tasksFields.cell4: <code1>watch</code1> (long-lived process, e.g. a dev server) or <code1>oneShot</code1> (runs and exits).
tasks_tasksFields.cell5: Buttons that write to the process' stdin: <code1>key</code1>, <code1>label</code1>, optional <code1>icon</code1> (<code1>refresh</code1>, <code1>restart</code1>, <code1>stop</code1>, <code1>bolt</code1>) and <code1>primary</code1>.
tasks_tasksFields.cell6: Reload on save: <code1>paths</code1>, <code1>ignore</code1>, <code1>onChange</code1> (required — an <code1>interactiveKeys</code1> label or <code1>"__restart__"</code1>) and <code1>debounceMs</code1> (300). Leave it out for tools that already watch (Vite, Next).
tasks_tasksFields.cell7: <code1>begin</code1> / <code1>end</code1> regexes that swing the badge between <em1>building</em1> and <em1>running</em1>.
tasks_tasksFields.cell8: Named run variants (launch configs): <code1>name</code1>, extra <code1>args</code1> appended after the task's, and <code1>env</code1> merged into the process environment. A chip cycles them before you hit play.
tasks_tasksFields.p2: For an argument value containing spaces, use <strong1>separate items</strong1> in <code1>args</code1> (<code1>["--dart-define", "MSG=hello world"]</code1>). And the output tab does not survive an app restart — the task dies with it.

databases.title: Databases
databases.p1: Connections live per workspace in <code1>.cockpit/databases.json</code1>, plus any SQLite files Cockpit auto-detects in the project. SQLite, Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Redis, and MongoDB open as tabs: a table view for SQL and Redis, a collection browser for MongoDB. A <code1>.dbq</code1> file is a saved query you can commit and re-run.
databases.p2: The same connections are reachable from the CLI, and the output is <strong1>one JSON line</strong1> — built to be parsed by an agent, not read by a human.
databases.p3: Each connection carries an <code1>access</code1> level (<code1>read</code1> — the default, including for connections created before the field existed — or <code1>readwrite</code1>) and an <code1>agents</code1> flag. A connection with <code1>agents: false</code1> is invisible to the CLI. The gates are enforced on the CLI surface: what you do by hand in the GUI is never blocked, but what an agent can reach is yours to decide. Run <code1>cockpit db --help</code1> for the full surface.

documents.title: Documents as tabs
documents.p1: Besides terminals, a Cockpit tab can be a document. Each one is a plain file in your repository, so git sees it, your agent can write it from the CLI, and nothing is locked inside the app. The <strong1>Gallery</strong1> panel, next to Database, has one card per document type: click it and the file is created at the workspace root and opened, on local and remote workspaces alike.

documents_documentsNotebook.title: Notebook (.notebook)
documents_documentsNotebook.p1: A folder whose name ends in <code1>.notebook</code1> is a notebook: one <code1>.md</code1> per note, each with a shallow YAML frontmatter. Cockpit shows the folder as a single item in the tree and opens it as a notes tab. Outside the app it is an ordinary folder, so git, Obsidian and an agent in the terminal read the same files.
documents_documentsNotebook.td2: Without it, the title is the file name minus .md
documents_documentsNotebook.cell1: A list <code1>[a, b]</code1>. With none, the note lands in the “no tag” group
documents_documentsNotebook.td6: Rewritten by the app on save
documents_documentsNotebook.p2: The parser never throws: a file with no frontmatter, or with an unterminated <code1>---</code1>, becomes a note whose body is the whole content. The app only rewrites the <code1>title</code1>, <code1>tags</code1> and <code1>updated</code1> lines, leaving the body and any other key untouched.
documents_documentsNotebook.p3: Notes are always editable, in a single mode: the markdown is painted live as you type while the markers stay visible, so the file remains plain markdown. It saves on its own about a second and a half after you stop typing (and on tab change or close), and ⌘S forces it. Pasting or dropping an image writes it to <code1>_assets/</code1> inside the notebook. <code1>[[Note title]]</code1> in the body becomes a clickable chip, creating the note if it does not exist, and each note lists its backlinks at the bottom.
documents_documentsNotebook.p4: The CLI always adds the reserved tag <code1>agent</code1> to a note it writes, and the UI marks those with a spark, so a note left by an agent is never confused with one you wrote.

documents_documentsHttp.title: HTTP requests (.http)
documents_documentsHttp.p1: A <code1>.http</code1> file is a request tab: editor on one side, response on the other. The syntax is the one the REST Client and JetBrains HTTP Client use, so files you already have work here: <code1>###</code1> separates requests, <code1>@name = value</code1> declares a variable and <code1>'{{'name'}}'</code1> interpolates it. Run the request under the cursor with ⌘↵ and read the response as JSON, as headers or as raw text.
documents_documentsHttp.p2: The agent runs the same file through the CLI, and gets one JSON line back. A 4xx or 5xx is a normal response, so it should check <code1>status</code1> rather than the exit code.

documents_documentsMore.title: Boards, diagrams and windows
documents_documentsMore.li1: <strong1>Kanban</strong1>: a <code1>.kanban</code1> markdown file renders as a board, with dependencies between cards (<code1>blockedBy</code1>, plus blocked and ready filters), a title and label filter, drag and drop in list mode, markdown in comments, and a hold on the advance arrow to send a card straight to the last column.
documents_documentsMore.li2: <strong1>Mermaid</strong1>: a <code1>```mermaid</code1> fence renders as a diagram in the markdown preview, offline, in your theme. Prefer it over ASCII art when an agent explains a flow.
documents_documentsMore.li3: <strong1>Document window</strong1>: open any file in its own light window from the app, or straight from the operating system. Double-click a <code1>.kanban</code1>, <code1>.notebook</code1>, <code1>.ckp</code1>, <code1>.dbq</code1>, <code1>.http</code1> or a markdown file in Finder, in Explorer or in your Linux file manager, and Cockpit opens it, forwarding the path to the instance you already have running.

env.title: Workspace environment (.env.cockpit)
env.p1: A plain <code1>KEY=VALUE</code1> file named <code1>.env.cockpit</code1> at the workspace root is injected into every terminal Cockpit opens there: every root of a multi-root workspace, and remote workspaces too, where the host reads its own copy right before spawning the shell. Put the tokens your agents need there instead of pasting them into a prompt. New tabs pick up changes, and <strong1>Restart</strong1> reloads an existing tab in place.

env_envRedaction.title: Redaction
env_envRedaction.p1: Values injected from the file are replaced by <code1>***</code1> before the output reaches the emulator, which covers the screen, the saved scrollback and <code1>cockpit read-tab</code1> at once. An agent reading another tab does not read your secrets back.
env_envRedaction.p2: Out of scope, on purpose: a value that the program re-encodes (base64, for instance) or splits with ANSI escapes, and the file itself, which is an ordinary file that anything with your permissions can read.

env_envBlocked.title: Keys that are never injected
env_envBlocked.p1: Keys that change <em1>who runs what</em1> are ignored, so a file that arrives with a repository cannot redirect the programs your shell starts:
env_envBlocked.p2: On top of that, when the <code1>.env.cockpit</code1> is tracked by git (so it came with the repository, it is not yours), new terminals print a notice listing the key <em1>names</em1> it injected, never the values. The Gallery card that creates the file also keeps it out of git.

env_envAccounts.title: A personal and a work account, side by side
env_envAccounts.p1: Claude Code and Codex read their whole account (credentials, settings and history) from a directory you can point somewhere else, and Cockpit injects those variables per workspace like any other. That is the recipe for separate accounts: no extra feature, one line per workspace.
env_envAccounts.p2: Restart the tabs (or open new ones), run <code1>claude</code1> and log in once with <code1>/login</code1>. From then on that workspace uses that account, and your other workspaces keep the default one. Use absolute paths: the variables name a directory, not a profile.

themes.title: Themes
themes.p1: Cockpit ships nine built-in themes — <code1>cockpit</code1>, <code1>cockpit.2</code1>, <code1>violet</code1>, <code1>violet.2</code1>, <code1>midnight</code1>, <code1>rose</code1>, <code1>sun</code1>, <code1>flexoki</code1> and <code1>pantera</code1> — each with a light and a dark variant. Beyond those, a theme is <strong1>a single JSON file</strong1> that paints all three layers at once: the app UI, the code viewer's syntax highlighting, and the terminal palette.

themes_themesFile.title: The theme file
themes_themesFile.li2: Themes live in <code1>'<'data folder'>'/themes/</code1> (the same root as the “Storage” setting), one file per theme, named after its <code1>id</code1>. Copying a <code1>.json</code1> in there installs it too.
themes_themesFile.li3: Export produces a <strong1>complete</strong1> file (every token, no <code1>extends</code1>) — a good starting point for hand editing.
themes_themesFile.cell1: Stable, namespaced identity (<code1>publisher.name</code1>). It is what gets stored in preferences, so renaming <code1>name</code1> never loses the user's choice. Cannot collide with a built-in id.
themes_themesFile.td3: What shows up in the picker.
themes_themesFile.cell2: Id of a built-in theme to inherit from. Absent = inherits from <code1>cockpit</code1>.
themes_themesFile.cell3: At least one of <code1>dark</code1> / <code1>light</code1>. A dark-only theme is applied in light mode too — better than mixing half a light theme with half a dark one.
themes_themesFile.p1: <strong1>Inheritance is the point.</strong1> Every token you do not declare comes from the base, so a useful theme can be five lines long:
themes_themesFile.p2: Colors are CSS-style hex — <code1>#RGB</code1>, <code1>#RRGGBB</code1> or <code1>#RRGGBBAA</code1>, <strong1>alpha last</strong1>. It is not Dart's <code1>0xAARRGGBB</code1>. On a bad import the parser points at the <strong1>field path</strong1> that broke (<code1>variants.dark.ui.accent</code1>), and validation runs before the copy, so an invalid file never reaches the themes folder.

themes_themesTokens.title: Tokens
themes_themesTokens.cell1: Surfaces <code1>bg</code1> <code1>panel</code1> <code1>panel2</code1> <code1>panel3</code1> · strokes <code1>border</code1> <code1>border2</code1> · text <code1>text</code1> <code1>text2</code1> <code1>text3</code1> <code1>text4</code1> · brand <code1>accent</code1> <code1>accentSoft</code1> <code1>accentText</code1> · state <code1>online</code1> <code1>ok</code1> <code1>error</code1> <code1>warn</code1> · editing <code1>edited</code1> <code1>editedBg</code1> · git <code1>gitStaged</code1> <code1>gitUntracked</code1> <code1>gitDeleted</code1> <code1>gitConflict</code1> · overlay <code1>scrim</code1> <code1>shadow</code1>
themes_themesTokens.cell2: <code1>cursor</code1> <code1>selection</code1> <code1>foreground</code1> <code1>background</code1>, the 8 normal ANSI colors, their 8 <code1>bright*</code1> counterparts, and <code1>searchHitBackground</code1> <code1>searchHitBackgroundCurrent</code1> <code1>searchHitForeground</code1>
themes_themesTokens.p1: Text drawn <em1>on top of</em1> <code1>accent</code1> and <code1>error</code1> is not a token: it is derived from the color's luminance, so a light accent automatically gets dark text.
themes_themesTokens.p2: <code1>syntax.background</code1> has a special default. The code viewer, the editor, and the terminal are all content inside a tab, so they share the field: when a theme declares neither <code1>syntax.background</code1> nor <code1>terminal.background</code1>, the three follow <code1>ui.panel</code1> of <em1>this</em1> theme, not of the base. Declare the field if your code palette needs a surface of its own.
themes_themesTokens.p3: The <code1>$schema</code1> URL lives in the repository, versioned next to the code that implements it, so the app and the schema can never drift apart. Cockpit ignores the field when reading a theme — it only serves your editor. See <a5><code1>theme.example.json</code1></a5> for a commented file with every group filled in.

turnStatus.title: Agent turn status
turnStatus.p1: When an agent runs in a tab, Cockpit shows whether it is <strong1>working</strong1>, <strong1>waiting</strong1> for you, or <strong1>idle</strong1> — as a spinner, a badge, a chime, and an OS notification when the window is unfocused. Supported harnesses today: <strong1>Claude Code</strong1> and <strong1>Codex CLI</strong1> (0.147+).
turnStatus.li1: At boot, Cockpit materializes the internal CLI at <code1>~/.cockpit/bin/cockpit</code1> and registers <code1>cockpit hook</code1> on the harness' lifecycle events.
turnStatus.li2: On each event the harness runs the hook, passing a JSON payload on stdin.
turnStatus.li3: The hook translates it into a status and sends it to the app over the local socket. (A socket rather than an escape sequence on the PTY: harnesses run hooks with no controlling terminal, and writing to <code1>/dev/tty</code1> fails with <code1>ENXIO</code1>.)
turnStatus.li4: Routing is by the <code1>COCKPIT_PANE_ID</code1> env var, which the app injects into the tab's PTY. An agent session started <em1>outside</em1> Cockpit does not have it, so the hook is a no-op there. Nothing to configure, nothing to disable.
turnStatus.cell2: Same shape, <strong1>plus</strong1> a trust block in <code1>~/.codex/config.toml</code1> (Codex silently ignores an untrusted hook, so Cockpit computes and writes the trust hash for you, between <code1># '>>>' cockpit hooks</code1> delimiters).
turnStatus.p3: Both installers do an <strong1>idempotent append</strong1> of a marked entry (<code1>_cockpit: v1</code1>): re-running removes our old entry and re-adds it, never rewriting the list — your own hooks, and those of plugins or iTerm2, survive untouched.

turnStatus_turnStatusEvents.title: Event mapping
turnStatus_turnStatusEvents.p1: Two asymmetries matter. On <strong1>Claude</strong1>, tools that block waiting for the user (<code1>AskUserQuestion</code1>, <code1>ExitPlanMode</code1>) emit no <code1>Notification</code1>; the last hook before the block is <code1>PreToolUse</code1>, so that one maps to <code1>waiting</code1> for those two — otherwise the tab would spin forever with no chime. On <strong1>Codex</strong1>, approval has its own event, so there is no text heuristic and no detour.

turnStatus_turnStatusResume.title: Resuming a session
turnStatus_turnStatusResume.p1: Cockpit persists the <code1>session_id</code1> that arrived through the hook, and on restoring the tab it types the command that reattaches the conversation. A session id alone does not say which harness it belongs to, and the commands differ — <code1>claude --resume '<'id'>'</code1> versus <code1>codex resume '<'id'>'</code1> — so the installer registers the hook as <code1>cockpit hook --harness '<'name'>'</code1> and the layout stores the harness next to the id. Entries written by older versions pass no flag and are assumed to be Claude, which is what they all were.
turnStatus_turnStatusResume.p2: The Codex trust key includes the hook's group index. If you add a hook of your own <em1>before</em1> ours on the same event — or edit <code1>hooks.json</code1> by hand — the hash stops matching and the hook silently stops running. The installer repairs it on the next boot, because it recomputes the indices from the final file.

remote.title: Remote hosts & VPS
remote.p1: A remote workspace is a folder on another machine, reached over SSH. Cockpit runs a small headless <code1>cockpit-server</code1> on the host, talks to it through an SSH tunnel to a Unix socket, and nothing is ever exposed on the network: SSH is the only door. Terminals and agents keep running on the host when you disconnect, and the next connection picks them up where they were.
remote.p2: From the <strong1>desktop</strong1> app you usually need nothing on the host: Cockpit uploads the server over SSH on first connect and keeps it updated (it compares a manifest of the installed files with the bundle it ships and reinstalls when they differ). The <strong1>mobile</strong1> apps (iPad, Android) carry no server, so a host you want to reach from them must be prepared once, either by a desktop or with the installer below.
remote.p3: The desktop can only install the targets it ships, so the installer is also the way in for the other combinations:
remote.p4: Both paths land in the same place and recognize each other: a host prepared with the installer is reused as is by a desktop that ships the same version, and a host prepared by a desktop can be updated later with the installer. Whoever gets there first installs; the other one just connects.

remote_remoteInstall.title: Install the server
remote_remoteInstall.p1: Linux x86_64 and arm64. User space, no sudo, idempotent; re-run it to update.
remote_remoteInstall.p2: The script detects the architecture, downloads <code1>cockpit-server-'<'version'>'-linux-'<'arch'>'.zip</code1> from the GitHub release, verifies its SHA-256 and runs the <code1>install.sh</code1> shipped inside the zip. That installs to <code1>~/.cockpit/server</code1> (the same layout the desktop app uses), links the binary into <code1>~/.local/bin</code1>, checks every file against <code1>bundle.manifest</code1> and does a smoke start before swapping the new version in. A host without internet access can take the zip by <code1>scp</code1> and run <code1>./cockpit-server/install.sh</code1> directly.
remote_remoteInstall.p3: <strong1>Versions must match.</strong1> Client and server are released together and the app refuses a different server version. Pin one with <code1>COCKPIT_VERSION=1.28.33</code1> in front of the command; without it the latest release is used. Desktop clients fix a mismatch by themselves over SSH; from mobile, re-run the installer.

remote_remoteService.title: Start at boot
remote_remoteService.p1: By default the app starts the server on demand and it exits when idle with no live session; terminals and agents keep the server alive while they run, so most hosts need no service. Note that if you kill the server while a Cockpit workspace is open on it, the client treats that as a dropped connection and starts it again. For a dedicated VPS you can register a <code1>systemd --user</code1> unit: the server is up right after a reboot, never exits on idle, and systemd restarts it on failure. It does not change how the app connects, and a reboot still ends the sessions that were running.
remote_remoteService.p2: The unit lives in <code1>~/.config/systemd/user/cockpit-server.service</code1>. Starting at boot without an open SSH session requires <em1>linger</em1>; the command tries to enable it and, when that needs root, prints the one-line <code1>sudo loginctl enable-linger</code1> for you to run once. Updates restart the unit automatically. To stop it for real use <code1>systemctl --user stop cockpit-server</code1> (a plain kill is undone by systemd in two seconds).

remote_remoteTroubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
remote_remoteTroubleshooting.li1: <strong1>version_mismatch</strong1>: the host runs another release than the app. Re-run the installer (mobile) or reconnect from a desktop, which reinstalls.
remote_remoteTroubleshooting.li2: <strong1>cockpit-server did not start</strong1> during install: the log printed above the error is the reason. A glibc older than the build expects is the usual cause on old distributions; check <code1>ldd --version</code1>.
remote_remoteTroubleshooting.li3: <strong1>Socket permission</strong1>: the server listens on <code1>~/.cockpit/cockpit-server.sock</code1> as the SSH user; connect with the same user that ran the installer.
remote_remoteTroubleshooting.li4: <strong1>Updating means restarting</strong1>: a new server version replaces the running process, which ends the terminals and agents on that host. The desktop does it silently when its bundle differs from the host; the installer does it when you run it with a newer release. Finish long jobs first.
remote_remoteTroubleshooting.li5: <strong1>Nothing after reboot</strong1>: without the service the first connection starts the server (a second or two); with it, check <code1>cockpit-server service status</code1> and linger.

sounds.title: Sounds & notifications
sounds.p1: Turn status drives audio too. Under <strong1>Settings → Notifications</strong1> you can bind a sound per event — <strong1>turn done</strong1>, <strong1>action needed</strong1>, <strong1>error</strong1> — pick a custom audio file for each, and set the volume. With the window focused you get the chime; unfocused, an OS notification. Since an agent started outside Cockpit never reports status, nothing fires for sessions the app is not hosting.

language.title: Language
language.p1: Cockpit's interface is fully localized in <strong1>English</strong1>, <strong1>Portuguese (Brazil)</strong1> and <strong1>Spanish</strong1>, down to the native application menu. Switch it in <strong1>Settings → General → Language</strong1>; the choice is independent of the OS locale.

intro.p1: Two small files turn “set up my environment” into one click: a <code1>.ckp</code1> layout that opens the right terminals in the right folders, and a <code1>.cockpit/tasks.json</code1> that runs your dev servers with buttons, profiles, and reload on save. Both live in the repository, so your teammates — and every new git worktree — get the same setup for free.

what.title: What you'll build
what.p1: A small monorepo with an API and a web app. By the end, opening the project gives you three terminals in the right folders, a task list with both servers ready to play, and a new worktree that recreates the whole thing by itself.
what.p2: Everything here is Cockpit-local: no account, no mesh, no agents required. If you want agents on top of this, follow <link1>An agent team in Cockpit</link1> next.

prereqs.title: Before you start
prereqs.li1: <strong1>Cockpit installed</strong1> — macOS, Windows, or Linux, from the <link2>download page</link2>.
prereqs.li2: A project folder open as a workspace. Anything with a couple of subfolders works; the commands below assume <code1>npm</code1>, but the runner is generic.

firstLayout.title: 1. Write your first layout
firstLayout.p1: Create <code1>dev.ckp</code1> at the root of the project. A layout is YAML, and the smallest useful one is three lines:
firstLayout.p2: Right-click the file in Cockpit's tree and choose <strong2>Open layout</strong2>. A tab named <code1>Agent</code1> opens at the project root and types <code1>claude</code1> for you. Apply it again: nothing happens. A pane whose <code1>name</code1> already exists is skipped, so a layout is safe to re-run and never closes anything.
firstLayout.p3: <code1>name</code1> becomes the tab's <strong2>stable label</strong2> — the one the <code1>cockpit</code1> CLI can address by name instead of by a boot-scoped id, and the same label you would otherwise set by double-clicking the tab.

splits.title: 2. Add splits and folders
splits.p1: Now the real geometry. <code1>cwd</code1> is relative to the <code1>.ckp</code1> file (forward slashes only, so the file works on every OS), and <code1>split</code1> says where each pane is born relative to the one created before it: <code1>tab</code1> (default), <code1>right</code1>, or <code1>down</code1>.
splits.p2: You can also apply it from inside any Cockpit terminal, which is how an agent sets up its own workspace:
splits.p3: That one line is the payoff. Every time you fork the workspace onto a fresh git worktree, Cockpit applies the layout by itself — and since a new worktree starts empty, the splits come out exactly as written. Keep a single autorun file at the root: with two or more, none of them runs, because ambiguity is never guessed.

tasks.title: 3. Declare your tasks
tasks.p1: Cockpit already detects tasks from <code1>package.json</code1> and <code1>pubspec.yaml</code1> with no configuration — open the Tasks panel and your scripts are there. You write <code1>.cockpit/tasks.json</code1> when you want more than that: a monorepo, interactive keys, environment profiles.
tasks.p2: The file goes at the root of the workspace you open — discovery is literal, with no walking up the tree. Each task's <code1>cwd</code1> is relative to that file, which is what lets one file at the monorepo root drive every subpackage. Hit play and the output streams into its own tab, with stop and restart controls and any <code1>interactiveKeys</code1> you declared as buttons that write straight to the process' stdin.
tasks.p3: <code1>profiles</code1> are launch configs: a chip cycles them before you press play, appending <code1>args</code1> and merging <code1>env</code1>. The runner stays generic on purpose — a Flutter flavor or a <code1>--dart-define</code1> is just more <code1>args</code1>.
tasks.p4: For a process that does not watch files itself (<code1>flutter run</code1> is the classic case), add a <code1>watch</code1> block: <code1>paths</code1> to observe, <code1>ignore</code1> to keep build folders from looping, and <code1>onChange</code1> pointing at an <code1>interactiveKeys</code1> label (<code1>"Hot reload"</code1>) or <code1>"__restart__"</code1>. Skip it for Vite or Next, which already reload on their own.

agents.title: 4. Let an agent use them
agents.p1: Both files are reachable from the internal <code1>cockpit</code1> CLI, which exists only inside Cockpit's terminals. That means an agent in one tab can start your dev server, read what it printed, and open a file for you to look at — without a screenshot or a screen scrape.
agents.p2: Task ids are stable per workspace: <code1>json:'<'label'>'</code1> for the ones you declared, <code1>npm:'<'script'>'</code1> and <code1>flutter:run</code1> for detected ones. The full command surface is in the <link3>Cockpit reference</link3>.

commit.title: 5. Commit them
commit.p1: Both files belong in git. <code1>dev.ckp</code1> is your working geometry, and <code1>.cockpit/tasks.json</code1> is how the project is run — the same reason a <code1>Makefile</code1> is committed. A teammate clones, opens the folder in Cockpit, and gets your terminals and your task list. Point <code1>$schema</code1> at <code1>tasks.schema.json</code1> from the repository and their editor will autocomplete the fields as well; Cockpit ignores the field when running.
commit.p2: From here: <link1>put a team of agents</link1> into those panes, or read the <link4>Cockpit reference</link4> for every field, flag, and the theme format.
