intro.p1: Cockpit's real power is the multiplexer: many agents in one window, each in its own folder. Here you wire up three, an <strong1>orchestrator</strong1>, a <strong1>backend</strong1> and a <strong1>frontend</strong1>, and let the orchestrator drive the other two with the internal <code1>cockpit</code1> CLI.

what.title: What you'll build
what.p1: Three agent tabs, side by side in a single Cockpit workspace. Each one is an ordinary terminal running your harness of choice (this tutorial uses <code1>claude</code1>; <code1>codex</code1> or <code1>pi</code1> work the same way), started in its own subfolder so it picks up that folder's brief and boots into a role.
what.p2: They coordinate through Cockpit itself. The orchestrator opens the worker tabs, types instructions into them and reads their output back, using the <code1>cockpit</code1> CLI that exists inside every Cockpit terminal. No network, no account, no extra service: it is the app you already have open, driven by the same verbs a human uses.
what.callout2: The CLI reference lives in the <link1>Cockpit docs</link1>, and <link2>Layouts and tasks</link2> shows how a <code1>.ckp</code1> file recreates a window like this one on any machine.

prereqs.title: Before you start
prereqs.li1: <strong1>Cockpit installed</strong1>, from the <link3>download page</link3>. Nothing else is required: Cockpit needs no account and no cloud.
prereqs.li2: <strong1>A harness on your PATH</strong1>, the one you already use. Cockpit runs it as a normal process, so whatever works in your terminal works in a tab.

folders.title: 1. Lay out the folders
folders.p1: An agent's identity comes from where it starts, so give each teammate a folder with its own brief:
folders.p2: <code1>AGENTS.md</code1> is the standing brief an agent reads when it starts in a folder (Claude Code also reads <code1>CLAUDE.md</code1>). Give each one a clear job, and tell the orchestrator how to reach the others.
folders.callout2: Keeping each agent in its own subfolder is what keeps the briefs, the histories and the edits apart. Three folders, three tabs, three roles.

tabs.title: 2. Open the three tabs
tabs.p1: Open <code1>my-app/</code1> as a workspace. Then open a terminal in each subfolder and start your harness there. The fastest way is from the Files panel: right-click a folder and open a terminal in it, then run <code1>claude</code1>.
tabs.p2: Split the canvas so all three are visible at once, the orchestrator on one side and the workers on the other, and rename each tab by double-clicking it: <code1>Orchestrator</code1>, <code1>Backend</code1>, <code1>Frontend</code1>. Those labels are how the CLI addresses a tab, and unlike ids they survive a restart of the app.
tabs.p3: Do it once by hand, or commit the whole geometry as a <code1>team.ckp</code1> and let Cockpit build the window for you:
tabs.callout2: Tab ids (<code1>t0</code1>, <code1>t1</code1>…) are handed out per app boot, so never hardcode one in a brief or a script. Address a tab by its label, or discover the id of the moment with <code1>cockpit list-tabs</code1>.

wiring.title: 3. Teach the orchestrator the CLI
wiring.p1: Every terminal Cockpit opens has <code1>cockpit</code1> on its <code1>PATH</code1>, and only those terminals do. So the orchestrator can already drive its teammates; it just needs to know the verbs. Ask it to look around:
wiring.p2: Four verbs are enough to run a team. If you use Claude Code, <code1>cockpit install-skill</code1> installs a skill that teaches all of them, so the brief can stay short.
wiring.callout2: A bare <code1>cockpit send</code1> types the text and leaves it in the composer. Use <code1>--enter</code1> (or a separate <code1>cockpit send-key Enter</code1>) to submit it, because a newline inside the text is a line break for the harness, not a send.

run.title: 4. Run the orchestration
run.p1: Now give the orchestrator something real. You talk only to it; it talks to the others.
run.p2: It breaks the work in two and types one instruction into each worker. The send returns as soon as the text is delivered, so it is a dispatch, not a blocking call:
run.p3: Each worker sees the instruction in its own tab, does the work <em1>in its own folder</em1>, and prints the result. The orchestrator polls for the turn to end, then reads the answer:
run.p4: With the contract in hand it unblocks the frontend, forwarding the exact shape, and reports the finished feature back to you. Three agents, three folders, one coordinated change, and you watched all of it happen.
run.callout2: You do not have to poll to know: each tab shows its own turn status (working, waiting on you, done), with a chime when the window is focused and a system notification when it is not. The same signal the orchestrator reads from <code1>working</code1> in <code1>list-tabs --json</code1>.

why.title: Why do this in Cockpit
why.p1: You could run three terminals, but then nothing connects them. Here the whole team lives in one window: every agent streams its own work in its own tab, the orchestrator dispatches and reads without you copying text around, and the layout comes back when you reopen the app. Add a terminal tab for the dev server, and the build, the agents and their traffic are all in front of you at once.
why.p2: From here: commit the <code1>.ckp</code1> and a <code1>.cockpit/tasks.json</code1> so a teammate gets the same window on clone (<link2>Layouts and tasks</link2>), or move the team onto a bigger machine and keep driving it over SSH (<link4>Remote hosts</link4>).

intro.h11: Telemetry: let agents query errors, not terminals
intro.p1: A dev server prints thousands of lines. Somewhere in there is the one error that matters, and the agent debugging your app has to read all of it to find it. Cockpit keeps a structured, per-workspace store of what your processes print, groups errors by fingerprint, and gives agents one CLI to ask <em1>what broke, where, and is it new</em1>. No SDK, no account, nothing leaves your machine.

what.title: What you get
what.li1: <strong1>A Telemetry tab</strong1> in the right panel (next to Files, Search, Database, Tasks): cases grouped by project and run, with counts, file:line, and tags for <em1>new</em1> and <em1>regression</em1>. Clicking a case opens it in the center pane with the stack, the JSON log printed right before it, occurrences per run, and the raw context lines.
what.li2: <strong1>Triage that agents respect.</strong1> Mark a case resolved and it disappears; if it comes back in a later run it returns flagged as a regression. Ignore a case and agents stop seeing it too.
what.li3: <strong1><code1>cockpit telemetry</code1></strong1>, a CLI that answers in compact JSON: errors, logs, one case in detail, wait-until-it-stops-happening.

how.title: 1. Where the data comes from
how.p1: Every task you run from <code1>.cockpit/tasks.json</code1> feeds the store by default. Anything else enters when you prefix the command with <code1>cockpit telemetry</code1>. That works in a terminal tab (colors and keys preserved) and from an agent’s own shell, which is the case that matters most: an agent running <code1>flutter test</code1> gets the three failing tests with file:line instead of the whole output.
how.callout1: Nothing is captured behind your back
how.callout2: Cockpit never taps a terminal you did not ask it to observe. Tasks are observed because Cockpit is the parent process; the wrapper is the explicit opt-in for everything else.

loop.title: 2. The agent loop
loop.p1: The wrapper prints a summary line at exit. From there the agent narrows down instead of reading up:
loop.p2: Useful filters: <code1>--new</code1> (never seen in earlier runs of the same command), <code1>--since-edit</code1> (since your last save in the editor), <code1>--before ev_xxxx --window 5s</code1> (what happened right before an event), <code1>--project</code1> in a monorepo. Replies are capped and tell the agent how to narrow further. The skill installed by <code1>cockpit install-skill</code1> teaches all of this to Claude Code and friends.

speak.title: 3. Make your project speak telemetry
speak.p1: Stack traces and error blocks are recognized as they are (Dart, Flutter, Node, Python, Rust, Go, test runners). For everything else there is one rule: make the project’s logger emit <strong1>JSON Lines</strong1> to stdout. Every ecosystem already does this (pino, structlog, slog, tracing). Cockpit only knows the field aliases:
speak.p2: Keep <code1>msg</code1> fixed and put variable data in fields: <code1>"msg":"order failed","orderId":"91c"</code1> groups into one case; <code1>"order 91c failed"</code1> becomes one case per order.
speak.callout1: Do not gate logs on Cockpit
speak.callout2: The app should behave the same inside and outside Cockpit. Control verbosity with your own knob (<code1>LOG_LEVEL</code1>, <code1>kReleaseMode</code1>), set per task through <code1>env</code1>. A <code1>COCKPIT=1</code1> check would not even reach a phone or a container.

extras.title: 4. Flutter, OpenTelemetry, HTTP proxy
extras.li1: <strong1>Flutter, zero code.</strong1> When a run prints the Dart VM Service URI, Cockpit attaches as a second client and reads <code1>dart:developer log()</code1> records and the framework’s structured errors. An error that also reached the console counts once.
extras.li2: <strong1>OpenTelemetry.</strong1> Observed processes get <code1>OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT</code1> and <code1>OTEL_SERVICE_NAME</code1> in their environment. An app with the OTel SDK (or Node’s auto-instrumentation) sends logs and spans to a local, loopback-only receiver; failed spans become cases too.
extras.li3: <strong1>HTTP proxy.</strong1> Point the frontend at the proxy port and every request/response is recorded with status, duration, redacted bodies and an injected <code1>x-request-id</code1>. Mark a reproduction window and replay it after the fix.

privacy.title: Privacy and retention
privacy.p1: The store is a SQLite file per workspace in Cockpit’s local cache, never inside your repository and never synchronized. Secrets are redacted on the way in (authorization headers, cookies, tokens, JWTs, passwords). Old runs are dropped after 7 days or 256 MB, oldest first. Delete anything from the Telemetry tab at any time.
privacy.p2: From here: put <link1>a team of agents</link1> on top of it, or read the <link2>Cockpit reference</link2>.

intro.p1: By the end of this guide you'll have Remote Pi running on one machine, your phone paired to it, and your first command sent from the app — the agent runs it and the result streams back to your pocket. Plan on about five minutes.

prereqs.title: Before you start
prereqs.li1: A machine with <strong1>Pi</strong1> (the coding agent) and <strong1>Node 20+</strong1> installed.
prereqs.li2: The <strong1>Remote Pi</strong1> app on your phone — from the <a1>App Store</a1>, <a2>Google Play</a2>, or the <link1>Android APK</link1> direct download.
prereqs.p2: No Pi yet? The <strong1>No Pi yet</strong1> tab below runs a one-command <code1>curl</code1> installer that sets up Pi, the plugin, and the supervisor for you. Already have Pi? Use the <strong1>Already have Pi</strong1> path.

install.title: 1. Install the plugin
install.p1: Remote Pi is a Pi plugin. Add it, run the setup wizard, then show a pairing QR:
install.callout2: Run <code1>/remote-pi</code1> before <code1>/remote-pi pair</code1>. On a brand-new folder with no config, <code1>pair</code1> will tell you to run the wizard first — that's the config step doing its job.

install_piInstallNpmremotePi.title: pi install npm:remote-pi
install_piInstallNpmremotePi.p1: Installs the plugin into Pi. This registers the <code1>/remote-pi</code1> slash command and deploys the agent-network skill that teaches the LLM the mesh tools.

install_remotePi.title: /remote-pi
install_remotePi.p1: The first run opens a short wizard that <strong1>creates the config for this folder</strong1>. It asks two questions:
install_remotePi.li1: <strong1>Agent name</strong1> — how other peers address this agent. Defaults to the folder name.
install_remotePi.li2: <strong1>Use the relay?</strong1> — answer <code1>Yes</code1> so your phone (and, later, other PCs) can reach this agent.
install_remotePi.p2: When it finishes, the agent has joined the local mesh and the relay is connected.

install_remotePiPair.title: /remote-pi pair
install_remotePiPair.p1: Prints a QR code (and a copy-paste pairing URI). Leave it on screen for the next step. Pairing is <strong1>per machine</strong1>: once a phone is paired, every Pi agent on this machine accepts it.

pair.title: 2. Pair your phone
pair.li1: Open the Remote Pi app on your phone.
pair.li2: Tap <strong1>Pair a device</strong1> (or the scan button) and point the camera at the QR.
pair.li3: The app confirms the pairing and the agent shows up in your device list. The Pi terminal footer flips to <code1>🟢 relay</code1> and shows <code1>📱 '<'shortid'>'</code1> while the phone is connected.
pair.p2: Pairing authenticates the two sides to each other with Ed25519, and all relay traffic is encrypted in transit (TLS).

firstCommand.title: 3. Send your first command
firstCommand.p1: You're now driving the agent from your phone. In the app's chat for this agent, type a prompt and send it:
firstCommand.p2: The prompt lands in the Pi session on your machine exactly as if you had typed it there. The agent runs, and its response streams back to your phone live. That round trip — phone to agent and back — is the whole point of Remote Pi.
firstCommand.p3: Beyond chatting, the app can drive the session with a few typed actions: <strong1>compact context</strong1>, <strong1>new session</strong1>, <strong1>set model</strong1>, and <strong1>set thinking</strong1> level. The model picker reads live from the host, so it always reflects what that machine can actually run.

next.li1: <link2>Local mesh</link2> — two agents on the same machine discovering and messaging each other.
next.li2: <link3>Daemon mode</link3> — promote a folder to a 24/7 background agent.

intro.p1: Two agents running side by side on one machine can see each other and trade messages — no network involved. Here you'll start a second agent, have the first one find it, and watch a message go from one to the other and back.

how.title: How local discovery works
how.p1: Every agent that runs <code1>/remote-pi</code1> on a machine joins the same local session, named <code1>local</code1>. They meet through a Unix domain socket — a local broker at <code1>~/.pi/remote/sessions/local/broker.sock</code1> — so messages never leave the box. The first agent to start hosts the broker; the rest connect to it. If the host exits, another agent takes over automatically.
how.callout2: A lock allows exactly one Pi agent per directory. To run two agents at once, put them in <strong1>two different folders</strong1> — each gets its own workspace, both meet in the <code1>local</code1> session.

start.title: 1. Start a second agent
start.p1: You already have one agent from the <link1>getting started</link1> guide. Open a second terminal in a <strong1>different</strong1> folder and start Remote Pi there too:
start.p2: Say the first agent is named <code1>agent-a</code1> and the second <code1>agent-b</code1> (the wizard defaults to the folder name). Both are now in the <code1>local</code1> session.

tools.title: 2. The three mesh tools
tools.p1: The agent-network skill gives the LLM three tools. You don't call them by hand — you ask the agent in plain language and it calls them for you.
tools.li1: <code1>list_peers()</code1> — who is online right now. Returns the peer names, one per line.
tools.li2: <code1>agent_send('{' to, body, re? '}')</code1> — send a message and wait for an ACK. Set <code1>re</code1> when you're replying to an earlier message.
tools.li3: <code1>get_messages()</code1> — drain this agent's inbox. The agent checks it at the start of each turn, so incoming messages surface on its next reply.

exchange.title: 3. Send a message across
exchange.p1: In <code1>agent-a</code1>''s terminal, ask it to find its peers:
exchange.p2: The LLM calls the tool and gets back the roster:
exchange.p4: <code1>Delivered</code1> means <code1>agent-b</code1>''s inbox accepted the envelope. On its next turn, <code1>agent-b</code1> sees it. Ask it:
exchange.p5: Back in <code1>agent-a</code1>, the <code1>pong</code1> shows up on its next turn, carrying <code1>re=ab12cd34</code1> so the agent knows which message it answers. The whole exchange is event-driven — nothing blocks waiting for a reply.

acks.title: Reading the ACK
acks.p1: <code1>agent_send</code1> tells you what happened to the envelope:
acks.li2: <code1>busy</code1> — the peer is mid-turn; the message was dropped. Retry shortly.
acks.li3: <code1>denied</code1> — the peer refused it. Don't retry.
acks.li4: <strong1>No ACK (timeout)</strong1> — the peer may be offline.
acks.callout1: A send is not a request
acks.callout2: <code1>agent_send</code1> is fire-and-ACK, not RPC. There is no obligation for the other agent to reply. If you need an answer, the prompt to the receiver has to ask for one — like <code1>reply to the sender</code1> above.

meta.title: Local mesh
meta.description: Run two Pi agents on the same machine and have them discover each other and exchange messages over the local broker with list_peers, agent_send, and get_messages.

intro.p1: The <link1>local mesh</link1> stops at one machine. Turn on the relay and the same <code1>agent_send</code1> reaches agents on other PCs — your laptop talking to your desktop, a build box, a server. The tools are identical; only the addressing changes.

setup.title: 1. Put both machines on one mesh
setup.p1: Cross-PC routing rides the relay. Every machine paired under the same <strong1>Owner key</strong1> forms one logical mesh — there is no central server, just a relay forwarding between paired peers. To get there:
setup.li1: On each machine, run <code1>/remote-pi</code1> and answer <strong1>Yes</strong1> to using the relay.
setup.li2: Pair both machines to the <strong1>same Owner</strong1> so they share one mesh. The mesh-membership details — how the Owner key signs the device list — live in <a1>PROTOCOL.md</a1>.
setup.p2: Point both machines at the same relay. The default is the community relay; for your own, see <link2>the relay reference</link2>.

addressing.title: 2. Address peers across PCs
addressing.p1: Once both machines are on the mesh, <code1>list_peers()</code1> shows local agents plus remote ones, each prefixed with the source machine's label:
addressing.p2: To message a remote peer, use its full <code1>pc_label:peer</code1> name verbatim — that's the only difference from a local send:
addressing.p3: The reply arrives the same way a local one does — in your inbox on a future turn, carrying <code1>re='<'your-send-id'>'</code1>.

delivered.title: 3. "Delivered" is not "alive"
delivered.p1: This is the one thing to internalize about remote sends. A <code1>Delivered</code1> ACK means <strong1>the remote broker accepted the envelope</strong1> — nothing more. It does <em1>not</em1> mean the peer is alive, processed the message, or will ever answer.
delivered.callout2: Don't treat <code1>Delivered</code1> as proof the other agent is working. <code1>list_peers</code1> can even list a peer that has gone stale. The only real confirmation is a <strong1>reply you actually receive</strong1>: ask the remote agent to respond, then wait for that envelope in your inbox. If it never comes, the peer may be offline regardless of what the ACK said.
delivered.p2: When a forwarded message genuinely can't be delivered, the relay returns a <code1>transport_error</code1> envelope with <code1>re='<'your-send-id'>'</code1> — watch your inbox for that too.

trust.title: What the relay sees
trust.p1: The relay is the only network-touching piece, so it's worth being precise about what it protects and what it doesn't:
trust.callout1: Encrypted in transit — payloads are not
trust.callout2: Connections to the relay are <strong1>encrypted in transit (TLS)</strong1>, and devices authenticate each other with <strong1>Ed25519 pairing</strong1>. But message payloads are <strong1>not</strong1> encrypted at the application layer — the relay operator could in principle read plaintext in memory while forwarding. If you need confidentiality from the relay operator, <link3>self-host the relay</link3> behind a VPN.
trust.p2: The community relay does not log, persist, or inspect payloads, but self-hosting is the way to get cryptographic-grade isolation. The full trust model is in <a1>PROTOCOL.md</a1>.

uses.title: What it's for
uses.p1: Cross-PC messaging lets you split work across roles that live on different machines — a <code1>frontend</code1> on your laptop handing tasks to a <code1>backend</code1> on a beefier box, or a <code1>tests</code1> agent on a build server reporting back. Same tools, same envelope; the relay just carries it between machines.

uses_KeepThemReachable.title: Keep them reachable
uses_KeepThemReachable.p1: Cross-PC coordination is most useful when the remote agents are always up. That's the next guide: <link4>run them as 24/7 daemons</link4>.

meta.title: Remote mesh
meta.description: Route messages between agents on different PCs through the relay, address peers as pc_label:peer, and understand what an ACK does and does not guarantee.

intro.p1: So far your agents only run while a terminal is open. Daemon mode keeps a folder running as a background agent that survives logout, restarts on crash, and answers your phone at 3am. This is the <em1>how</em1>; for the <em1>why</em1> — and how it compares to all-in-one platforms — see <link1>Why Pi</link1>.

model.title: The shape of it
model.p1: One <strong1>supervisor</strong1> runs per machine. Under it sit N background agents — one per folder you promote. The supervisor is a normal user service: <code1>launchd</code1> on macOS, <code1>systemd --user</code1> on Linux. It starts at login, survives reboots, and respawns any agent that crashes.
model.callout2: A daemon inherits the same Pi tool permissions your interactive session has — <code1>Bash</code1>, <code1>Edit</code1>, <code1>Write</code1> all run <strong1>without a prompt</strong1>, because no one is at the keyboard to approve them. Configure Pi's tool permissions to taste <em2>before</em2> you promote a folder to a 24/7 daemon. A tool-approval gate is on the roadmap.

install.title: 1. Install the supervisor (once per machine)
install.p2: That single command does two things:
install.li1: Installs and activates the user-level supervisor service (<code1>launchd</code1> / <code1>systemd --user</code1>), so it auto-starts at login and after reboot.
install.li2: Symlinks the <code1>remote-pi</code1> and <code1>pi-supervisord</code1> CLIs into <code1>~/.local/bin/</code1> so you can manage daemons from any shell. If that directory isn't on your <code1>$PATH</code1>, the command prints the line to add.
install.p3: This is a separate, explicit opt-in — it is <strong1>not</strong1> part of the regular setup wizard. You only run it on machines where you want 24/7 agents.

create.title: 2. Promote a folder to a daemon
create.p1: No per-folder setup is needed first — <code1>create</code1> registers any folder and the supervisor injects the daemon's config at spawn (a fixed <code1>assistent</code1> workspace, relay on), so the folder needs no <code1>.pi/remote-pi/</code1> of its own. To reach the daemon from your phone, just make sure this machine has been paired once — pairing is per-machine, so any earlier <code1>/remote-pi pair</code1> on it counts. Then register:
create.p2: The id is a stable hash of the folder path (<code1>sha256(realpath)[:8]</code1>), so it survives moves and is the same on every machine. With the supervisor running, <code1>create</code1> <strong1>starts the daemon right away</strong1> — there is no separate start step. It restarts on crash and comes back after a reboot on its own.
create.callout2: The by-path id rejects a second daemon in the same directory at <code1>create</code1> time. Pairing stays interactive — a daemon reuses the keypair and paired devices already set up on this machine; it doesn't show a QR itself.

fleet.title: 3. Manage the fleet
fleet.p1: Every command works as a Pi slash command (<code1>/remote-pi …</code1>) and, once the CLI is linked, as a plain shell command (<code1>remote-pi …</code1>):
fleet.p2: A daemon receives a prompt as if a user typed it; its response flows back through the same mesh and relay you configured — your phone sees it live, and other agents on the machine see it over the local mesh.

fleet_WhereTheLogsAre.title: Where the logs are
fleet_WhereTheLogsAre.p1: Each daemon's output is forwarded into the supervisor log with a <code1>['<'cwd'>']</code1> prefix, so one stream shows the whole fleet.

cron.title: 4. Schedule recurring prompts (cron)
cron.p1: A daemon only acts when something prompts it. <code1>cron</code1> lets the supervisor be that something on a schedule — “every weekday at 9am, summarize the new PRs” — with no one at the keyboard. Jobs target a daemon by id and survive reboots along with the supervisor.
cron.callout1: Cron needs the supervisor installed as a service
cron.callout2: The scheduler runs <em1>inside</em1> the supervisor, so it only fires when the supervisor is installed as a user service. Run <code1>/remote-pi install</code1> (step 1) first — without it, <code1>cron add</code1> warns instead of pretending to schedule. It is the same launchd / systemd service that keeps your daemons alive; there is no second scheduler.
cron.p2: With a daemon registered (step 2) and the supervisor running, add a job. The first argument is the daemon id, then a standard five-field cron expression, then the prompt:
cron.p3: Runs must be at least <strong1>60 seconds</strong1> apart — a more frequent expression is rejected with a clear message, since every fire spends tokens. Flags on <code1>cron add</code1>:
cron.li1: <code1>--tz Area/City</code1> — run in a specific, DST-aware timezone (e.g. <code1>America/Sao_Paulo</code1>). Defaults to the machine's local time.
cron.li2: <code1>--wake</code1> — if the daemon is stopped when the job fires, start it first, then send. Default: skip (logged as <code1>skipped_down</code1>).
cron.li3: <code1>--no-skip-busy</code1> — send even if the daemon is mid-turn. By default a fire is skipped while the daemon is still working (<code1>skipped_busy</code1>) so prompts don't pile up on an unfinished turn.
cron.li4: <code1>--catchup</code1> — after the supervisor was down, fire <em1>one</em1> missed run on startup. Default off; never replays the whole backlog.
cron.p4: Each job gets an id like <code1>j_ab12</code1> (printed by <code1>cron add</code1> and <code1>cron list</code1>). Inspect, test, and audit the fleet's schedule:
cron.p5: The agent's reply is fire-and-forget into the mesh — your phone and other agents see it live, exactly like a manual <code1>daemon send</code1>. Cron itself only audits the <em1>trigger</em1>: every fire and every skip appends one line to <code1>~/.pi/remote/cron.jsonl</code1>, which <code1>cron log</code1> tails. Full subcommand reference is in the <link2>docs</link2>.

cleanup.title: Removing a daemon
cleanup.p1: <code1>uninstall</code1> is reversible — re-running <code1>/remote-pi install</code1> later brings every registered daemon back. Full flags and paths are in the <link3>reference docs</link3>.

meta.title: Daemon mode
meta.description: Keep a Pi agent alive 24/7: install the supervisor (launchd / systemd --user), register a folder as a daemon, and manage the fleet from one CLI.

intro.span1: Extra · terminal only — no app yet
intro.p1: <code1>remote-pi claude</code1> puts <strong1>Claude Code</strong1> on the same agent mesh as Pi — a named peer on the local UDS broker and, through the relay, across PCs. This is an advanced, agent-to-agent setup driven entirely from the terminal. It is <strong1>not surfaced in the mobile app yet</strong1> — see <a1>why</a1> at the end.

prereqs.title: Before you start
prereqs.li1: The <code1>remote-pi</code1> CLI on your <code1>$PATH</code1> — run <code1>/remote-pi install</code1> once (see the <link1>daemon tutorial</link1>) to link it.
prereqs.li2: <strong1>Claude Code</strong1> installed and on your <code1>$PATH</code1> as <code1>claude</code1>.
prereqs.li3: A folder that <strong1>isn't</strong1> already running a Pi agent (see <a2>one agent per folder</a2>).

run.title: Run it
run.p1: On the first run in a folder, it asks for an agent name (defaulting to the folder name) and saves a small config:
run.p2: That name is how other agents address this Claude in <code1>list_peers</code1> and <code1>agent_send</code1>. Then it wires three things into Claude Code and launches it.

injected.title: What it wires in
injected.p1: <code1>remote-pi claude</code1> is a wrapper. It injects three things, then spawns <code1>claude</code1> in the target folder.

injected_mcp.title: 1. An MCP server (the mesh tools)
injected_mcp.p1: It registers a stdio MCP server named <code1>remote-pi-mesh</code1> in Claude's <strong1>local scope</strong1> — per-folder, stored in <code1>~/.claude.json</code1>, not written into the project directory and not committed to version control:
injected_mcp.label1: What the wrapper runs (you don't type this)
injected_mcp.p2: The server exposes three tools to Claude — the same mesh API Pi agents get:
injected_mcp.li1: <code1>list_peers</code1> — who is online: local peers plus cross-PC ones in <code1>pc_label:peer</code1> form (e.g. <code1>MacMini:backend</code1>).
injected_mcp.li2: <code1>agent_send('{' to, body, re? '}')</code1> — send a message and get an <strong1>ACK</strong1> back (<code1>received</code1>, <code1>busy</code1>, <code1>denied</code1>, or <code1>timeout</code1>). It is <strong1>not fire-and-forget</strong1>; set <code1>re</code1> to the id of the message you're replying to.
injected_mcp.li3: <code1>get_messages</code1> — drain this agent's inbox of pending messages.

injected_skill.title: 2. The agent-network skill
injected_skill.p1: An MCP server gives Claude the tools but not the <em1>habits</em1>. Skills load only from disk, so the wrapper deploys one to <code1>~/.claude/skills/agent-network/SKILL.md</code1>. The skill's description self-gates to mesh contexts, so it doesn't intrude on unrelated Claude sessions. It teaches Claude to:
injected_skill.li1: call <code1>get_messages</code1> at the start of every turn, so incoming messages are seen promptly;
injected_skill.li2: read the <code1>agent_send</code1> ACK and act on it (retry on <code1>busy</code1>, give up on <code1>denied</code1>) rather than assuming delivery;
injected_skill.li3: reply by echoing the original message id in <code1>re</code1>, so threads stay linked;
injected_skill.li4: treat <code1>broadcast</code1> as fire-and-forget — no per-recipient ACK.

injected_channels.title: 3. Channel push (wake on message)
injected_channels.p1: When a message lands, the MCP server emits a <code1>notifications/claude/channel</code1>. Whether that reaches Claude immediately depends on one launch flag:
injected_channels.li1: <strong1>Push</strong1> — with <code1>--dangerously-load-development-channels server:remote-pi-mesh</code1> on (the wrapper sets it), the notification <strong1>wakes Claude</strong1> right away, so it reacts to an incoming message without you prompting it.
injected_channels.li2: <strong1>Poll</strong1> — without that flag, Claude only sees the message the next time it calls <code1>get_messages</code1> (i.e. on its next turn).

flags.title: The --dangerously-* flags
flags.p1: The wrapper launches Claude with two flags:
flags.callout2: <code1>--dangerously-skip-permissions</code1> <strong1>auto-approves every tool call</strong1> — Claude runs Bash, edits, and writes without prompting you, which is what makes unattended agent-to-agent work possible but also removes your approval gate. <code1>--dangerously-load-development-channels</code1> opens a development channel for the local MCP server (it shows a one-time confirmation dialog at startup). Only point this at folders and peers you trust — same posture as promoting a folder to a <link1>daemon</link1>.

cwdLock.title: One agent per folder
cwdLock.p1: A kernel-enforced lock (the same one <code1>/remote-pi</code1> takes) allows <strong1>one remote-pi agent per folder</strong1> — Pi <em1>or</em1> Claude, never both in the same directory. If a folder already has a Pi agent, start Claude in a different folder; both still meet in the same local mesh. A second agent in a locked folder is refused before it connects, so it never becomes a ghost peer.

noApp.title: Why this isn't in the app yet
noApp.p1: The mobile app talks to the <strong1>relay</strong1>, and it sees only the Pi agent that paired it. It does not see local UDS peers — like a Claude joined with <code1>remote-pi claude</code1> — so a mesh-mate Claude won't show up in your phone. Surfacing the full mesh in the app is future work; for now this is a terminal-driven, agent-to-agent feature. Relay traffic, where it's used, is encrypted in transit.
noApp.p2: To watch two agents talk on one machine, pair this with the <link2>local mesh</link2> tutorial — start one peer as Pi and another as Claude, in two folders, and have them message each other.
